scenes.tts: In 1949 Pauling, with the physician Harvey Itano and the researchers S. J. Singer and Ibert Wells, ran healthy and sickle-cell hemoglobin through an electrophoresis cell and watched them drift at different speeds: the sickle protein carried a few extra units of positive charge.
scenes.visual: portrait inset; 1949 timeline, four named people, electrophoresis cell with healthy vs sickle drift, extra positive charge
scenes.narration: In 1949 Pauling, with the physician Harvey Itano and the researchers S. J. Singer and Ibert Wells, ran healthy and sickle-cell hemoglobin through an electrophoresis cell and watched them drift at different speeds: the sickle protein carried a few extra units of positive charge.

scenes.tts: Two molecules, one letter of difference, and one of them deforming red cells into crescents. He named it "a molecular disease," the first time anyone pinned a specific human illness to a specific defect in a specific molecule.
scenes.visual: one-letter-different strips, red cell to crescent, 'a molecular disease', illness-defect-molecule chain
scenes.narration: Two molecules, one letter of difference, and one of them deforming red cells into crescents. He named it "a molecular disease," the first time anyone pinned a specific human illness to a specific defect in a specific molecule.

scenes.tts: Vernon Ingram later located the exact lesion, glutamate to valine at position 6 of the β chain — the very mutation on this deck's sickle-cell slide — but the conceptual leap was Pauling's, and every mutation-targeted drug since works from that one phrase.
scenes.visual: Ingram later, beta chain position 6 glutamate to valine, conceptual leap -> a molecular disease -> drugs

scenes.tts: His alpha-helix remark, sketched from a sickbed in Oxford in 1948, came from the same habit of reading structure off behavior: "I was so pleased with this structure that I stayed up until late in the night, pondering about it."
